schools.summary: Gill states three uses for the list: it shows the original of the several nations, it confutes the pretended antiquity of the Egyptians, Chaldeans and Chinese, and it points out the people who were to be the seat of the church and from whom the Messiah should spring, which he takes for the principal view of the history. Calvin declines the enquiry into particular nations, saying he does not condemn the industry of those who pursue it and will let them enjoy the reward of their labours; what interests him is that in these bare names we still hold a fragment of the world's history, and that so many forgot it, the memory of the deluge being lost by most and the door thereby opened to the fables of the heathen poets.

Henry asks why Japheth is treated first and answers either that he was the eldest or that his family lay remotest from Israel, so that his race is dispatched briefly while Moses hastens to Ham, Israel's enemies, and Shem, Israel's ancestors; for it is the church that Scripture is designed to be the history of. He marks that the sons were born after the flood, to rebuild the world of mankind the flood had ruined, and reads the allotment of the isles of the Gentiles as probably including Britain, taking the promise that the isles shall wait for his law of the conversion of the Gentiles. He sets a limit too: no nation except the Jews can be sure which of these seventy it came from, the lists having been kept among them alone for the sake of the Messiah.

Clarke enters the sharpest caution in the chapter, that it is extremely difficult to say what peoples sprang from the three grand divisions since most of these names have changed in the lapse from the deluge to the Christian era; his main point is that Moses names not the first settler but the people from whom the country afterwards took its name, Mizraim being a dual and Kittim, Dodanim, Ludim, Philistim and Caphtorim plurals, while among Canaan's posterity whole nations stand in place of the men they sprang from and even place-names are entered instead of settlers. He also passes on, without vouching for it, the report that Noah made a will bequeathing the East to Shem, Africa to Ham and Europe to Japheth.

Keil and Delitzsch pair the chapter with the next, the genealogy tracing the origin of the scattered tribes and the confusion of tongues giving the cause of their division, and defend the record as no ethnographical myth nor an ancient Hebrew's attempt to connect his people with the world by uncertain traditions, but a historical account resting on a tradition from the fathers which by its contents belongs to the age of Abraham. Ellicott adds that Shem, Ham and Japheth stand in that undeviating order throughout.

themes: the generations of the sons of Noah
how far the descent of nations can be traced

2.pericope_label: The sons of Japheth and the isles of the Gentiles

schools.summary: Gill observes that Japheth, named last, is treated first, by the figure rhetoricians call a chiasm, reports from Josephus that his sons settled from Taurus and Amanus east to the Tanais and west to Gadira, and has Gomer father the Gomerites whom the Greeks called Galatians, the Gauls of Asia Minor who held Phrygia. On the isles he argues the word cannot mean islands proper, which would not have held Japheth's posterity and which men would hardly have sought when shipping was little known, since the Hebrews called all places reached by sea or lying on the coast islands; the phrase is better rendered the countries of the Gentiles.

Clarke identifies Japheth with the Japetus of the Greeks and assigns Magog to the Scythians and Tartars, Javan to the Ionians, Tiras to the Thracians, Tubal to the Iberians and Meshech to the Cappadocians, but balks at Madai, where the Medes are the usual answer while Joseph Mede makes the Macedonian Maedi probable, and concludes that nothing certain can be advanced. On Gomer's sons he suggests Sacagena for Ashkenaz and the Paphlagonians for Riphath, and on Javan's he makes Tarshish Cilicia, whose capital was the Tarsus where Paul was born, and offers Dodona, Rhodes or the Rhone for Dodanim. Wesley keeps only that the allotment was made by lot after a survey.

Keil and Delitzsch canvass the old Jewish explanation of Ashkenaz as the Germani and Knobel's family of Asi before reporting that Kiepert and Bochart decide for the Ascanians of northern Phrygia, give Knobel's Celts and Josephus's Paphlagonia for Riphath while calling both very uncertain, and note that the Armenians still call themselves the house of Thorgom; on Tarshish they hold to the Spanish colony of Tartessus against Knobel's Etruscans, which Delitzsch objects were probably of Lydian and so Shemite descent. Ellicott is bolder throughout, making Gomer the Cimmerians who left their name in the Crimea before becoming the Cimbri of Denmark and the Cymry of Wales, Magog the Scythians represented now by the Russians, and Tiras the Thracians and so the Scandinavians; he thinks Tartessus too late a foundation and prefers the Tyrseni, says no dependence can be placed on the reading Dodanim, and remarks that the extension of Japheth eastward into Parthia, Bactria and India was as remarkable as westward.

6.pericope_label: Ham, Cush, and the rise of Nimrod

schools.summary: Gill quotes Josephus that Ham's sons held from Syria and the mountains to the sea, and adds that many of their names are lost and others so bent into other tongues as to be scarcely recognisable. Calvin sets Nimrod against the moderation of his age, when men of dignity governed by civil laws and had more authority than power, and finds him branded with an eternal mark of infamy, from which we learn how pleasing to God a mild administration is.

Henry takes Nimrod for a tyrant in the making: those before him were content to stand level with their neighbours, but his aspiring mind would lord it over them, the spirit of the giants before the flood reviving in him so soon after that judgment. His hunting Henry reads two ways, either that he rid the country of wild beasts and so won his neighbours' affection, or that under that pretence he gathered armed men and became a violent invader of their rights; he thought himself a mighty prince, but before the Lord he was only a mighty hunter, and great conquerors are but great hunters, Alexander appearing in prophecy as no more than a he-goat pushing.

Clarke keeps to a line apiece on the sons of Ham, derives Nimrod's name from a root meaning to rebel, and piles up the Targums, which make him a hunter of men and a rebel before the Lord. Wesley follows Henry on the ambition and the hunting alike.

Keil and Delitzsch trace the Egyptian Kemi to Ham rather than to Plutarch's ash-grey Nile silt, take the dual Mizraim for Upper and Lower Egypt while calling the name untraceable to any Semitic root, scatter the Cushites over southern Asia with an original settlement in Arabia, and place Cush's five sons from Meroe to Caramania; they read the Greek of the ninth verse as against Jehovah rather than before him. Ellicott prefers Chemi, the old name of Egypt, to the derivation of Ham from a root meaning sunburnt, puts the Cushite home on the Tigris and Euphrates, cites Brugsch-Bey's conclusion from mummy skulls that the ancient Egyptians were Caucasian of a Cushite branch cradled in Central Asia, and notes that the southern half of Arabia was Cushite when the table was written while their chief home was Mesopotamia. He alone defends Nimrod, calling the explanation of Hamite names by Hebrew roots unscholarlike and the traditions that blacken him no older than Josephus.

debates.question: Was Nimrod a tyrant or a benefactor?

sides.position: a tyrant; the name means rebel, the Targums make him a hunter of men, and Moses brands him with lasting infamy
a public benefactor who organised the hunt and brought order among scattered men; the rebel etymology is unscholarlike and the hostile traditions date only from Josephus

themes: Cush in Asia and in Africa
he began to be a mighty one in the earth
a mighty hunter before the Lord

10.pericope_label: Babel, Nineveh, and the question of Asshur

schools.summary: Gill defends Nimrod's title to Babel against the classical writers who gave it to Semiramis or Ninus, holding with Berosus and Abydenus that Belus built it and that Belus is Nimrod, and concludes that the whole notice of Nimrod is written by anticipation, since he was no powerful prince until after Babel was built and the languages confounded. On the eleventh verse he lays the question out squarely, whether Asshur is a man's name or a country's, listing Onkelos, Junius, Piscator and Bochart with the English margin for the country, and noting that those who take that route give a better reason than the Targumist, namely that Nimrod made war on Assyria and seized it. Calvin will not have Babylon made as grand as the profane historians do, suspecting the region's fruitfulness invited later hands to enlarge it until Aristotle compared it to a province; he reports with sympathy the view that Asshur was of the posterity of Shem and was violently expelled by Nimrod, which would mark the tyrant's ferocity and illustrate the proverb that great kingdoms are great robberies, yet he too adopts the reading that makes Asshur a country.

Clarke observes that Babel means confusion, a proper name for a kingdom founded in apostasy and supported by tyranny and rapine, prefers the marginal reading that sends Nimrod into Assyria, and thinks Ninus, from whom Nineveh is supposedly named, probably Nimrod himself; of Rehoboth and Calah nothing certain is known. Wesley reads the verse for what it shows about government, that Nimrod had no apparent right to rule by birth and either his fitness recommended him or power and policy advanced him, which he takes for the antiquity of civil government and of that form which lodges sovereignty in a single person.

Ellicott takes Babel for Bab-ili, the gate of God, a literal Assyrian rendering of the older Accadian name, the derivation from a root for confusion belonging to the next chapter and being derisive; he identifies Shinar with Babylonia, called Sumir in the inscriptions and named the land of Nimrod by Micah, and brings Erech into the light of the tablets as Urak, ravaged by an Elamite king, now Warka. Keil and Delitzsch make the four Assyrian places one composite city carrying the name of Nineveh, so that the great city at the end describes Nineveh rather than Resen.

debates.question: Is Asshur here a man or a country?

sides.position: a country; the sense is that Nimrod went out into Assyria and built there
a man of the posterity of Shem, driven out of his neighbourhood by Nimrod — reported as the received opinion, though not finally adopted

themes: the beginning of his kingdom was Babel
out of that land went forth Asshur

schools.summary: Gill insists that Ludim is not a man but a people, so that Mizraim begat the father of the Ludim, identifies them with the Lydians as against those of Asia Minor descended from Lud son of Shem, and follows Bochart in placing them in Africa as the Ethiopians now called Abyssines, adding that Diodorus Siculus shows the likeness between Egyptians and Ethiopians, who deified their kings alike and used hieroglyphics. He grants Justin's derivation of Sidon from the plenty of fish on that coast but holds that since Canaan had a son of the name the city was no doubt called from him, notes that Sidon is older than Tyre, which the Sidonians built, and that Homer mentions the one and not the other; of the peoples that follow he observes that the Jebusites gave Jerusalem its older name and held it until David, and places the Hivites in Hermon.

Henry asks why Canaan's posterity is described more particularly than any other family here, and answers that these were the nations to be subdued before Israel, whose land was in time to become Immanuel's land, God having an eye to that when he cast the lot of this devoted race in the very spot he had chosen for his own people. The harder point he draws out is that Canaan's posterity were numerous, rich and pleasantly situated, and yet under a divine curse, and not a curse causeless: those under the curse of God may still prosper greatly in this world, for we cannot know love or hatred by what is before us but by what is within us, and the curse always works really and terribly though it may work secretly.

Clarke works through Mizraim's descendants a line apiece, putting Ludim in the Mareotis, Anamim about the temple of Jupiter Ammon, Lehabim among the Libyans, Casluhim in Colchis, which almost all authors allow was peopled from Egypt, and Caphtorim in Cyprus after Calmet, while of Naphtuhim he says even conjecture can scarcely fix a place. Wesley states Henry's point as a comparison and leaves it there: Canaan has here a better land than either Shem or Japheth, and yet they have the better lot, for they inherit the blessing.

Keil and Delitzsch argue that Zidon here is a man and not the Phoenician capital, since the apposition his firstborn and the verb begat both require a person, since a city name would not harmonise with the other descendants, whose analogy calls for the gentile form Sidonian, and since the word, from a root meaning to hunt, does not suit a seaport; they take Heth the same way, a person from whom the Hittites are named.

themes: the plural names of Mizraim’s line
is Zidon a man or a city?
why Canaan is described most fully

21.pericope_label: Shem, the father of the children of Eber

schools.summary: Gill holds that for the sake of those whose father Shem is here called, this genealogy and indeed all of Genesis was written, since the Hebrews sprang from Eber in Shem's line, among whom the church was kept and from whom the Messiah came; on the name he reports Jarchi's reading of Eber as beyond the river but objects that this straitens Shem's posterity too much, since they lived on both sides. Calvin notices that Shem alone is given a preface and reads the exception as deliberate, this being the race chosen by God; the blessing does not descend to all his grandchildren indiscriminately but stays in one family, and although Eber's descendants fell away, so that God might justly have disinherited them, the benediction was only buried for a season until Abraham was called.

Henry finds two titles here. Shem is father of all the children of Eber, which he explains by Abraham's seed both descending from Eber and being called Hebrews after him; he supposes Eber eminent for religion in a time of general apostasy and thinks the holy tongue was probably kept in his family through the confusion of Babel as a token of God's favour, adding that though the people were despised bond-slaves in Egypt when Moses wrote, it was an honour to be akin to them. The second title, brother of Japheth the elder, shows that although Shem is commonly put first he was not Noah's firstborn.

Wesley follows Henry and asks why the brotherhood of Japheth should be part of Shem's description when it had been said already, answering that it signifies the union of the Gentiles with the Jews, lest Japheth's seed be thought shut out. Clarke breaks with all of them, holding it much more likely that the Hebrews took their name not from Eber but from Abraham's passing over the Euphrates into Canaan, since the verb means to pass over; he gives Elam to the Elamites, Asshur to the province that became an empire, Lud to the Lydians and Aram to the Arameans afterwards called Syrians.

Keil and Delitzsch work through Aram's four sons with their usual caution, associating Uz with Ptolemy's Aesitae and the country of Job while calling the Aramaean connection mere conjecture, and explain Peleg's name from the division of the earth's population after the tower, noting that his brother Joktan is reckoned by the Arabians the father of all their primitive tribes. Ellicott says the name Arphaxad at present defies all explanation, and observes that the table then turns to the Joktanite Arabs and omits the Hebrews, Eber's birth being recorded only to show where the primogeniture lay.

debates.question: Where does the name Hebrew come from?

sides.position: from Eber, whose name the holy tongue and the professors of religion both carried
more likely from Abram passing over the Euphrates, the verb meaning to pass over

themes: the father of all the children of Eber
the brother of Japheth the elder
in his days was the earth divided

26.pericope_label: The Joktanite Arabs and the division of the earth

schools.summary: Gill traces Joktan's sons mostly through Bochart and shows how thin the ground is: Hadoram is defended by a promontory that needs two letters transposed, Obal requires the family to cross the straits of the Arabian Gulf, and Abimael rests on a single place-name in Theophrastus, while Ophir is hardest of all, since placing him at Solomon's Ophir carries him too far from his brethren. He takes Mesha for the Muza of Ptolemy and Pliny, a Red Sea port frequented by the merchants of Egypt and Ethiopia, and Zephar for the Saphar lying eastward at the foot of Climax. Counting twenty-six names in Shem's branch he says at once there must have been many more, and on the closing verse insists the division was not immediate but waited until the families could form nations, until the days of Peleg and the building of the tower, whence they peopled all the known parts of the world and no doubt America; he hears an echo of the same partition in Pindar.

Clarke reports Calmet looking far north for the boundaries, to Mount Masius in Mesopotamia on one side and mountains in Armenia or Media on the other, and closes the chapter with an argument for the unity of mankind drawn from custom rather than names — reckoning by tens, counting time in weeks of seven days, keeping the seventh for religion, consecrating temples and altars, appointing places of refuge, giving a tenth of the produce to the altar, worshipping barefoot — usages so widely shared that they could only come from a common institution held before the dispersion.

Keil and Delitzsch say outright that Mesha is still unknown, rejecting as very improbable both Gesenius, who makes it Mesene on the Persian Gulf, and Knobel, who makes it a valley in northern Yemen, and report the conjecture that Sephar is the old Himyarite capital on the Indian Ocean; they read the last clause as a bridge to the event that turned one race into many nations with different tongues. Ellicott draws an inference from the phrase after their generations, that each family kept some record of its own descent and that this table was compiled by comparing many such records.
